title: Yoga-Based Cardiac Rehab Improved Quality of Life in Heart Failure Trial
excerpt: In 3,492 adults in India, Yoga-CaRe improved quality-of-life scores and walking distance, but death, hospitalisation or stroke was 21.0% versus 22.8% — not statistically significant.
body:
• In the Yoga-CaRe HF trial of 3,492 adults in India with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, yoga-based cardiac rehab improved quality-of-life scores by 8.06 points more than enhanced standard care at three months.
  • Participants in the yoga group also walked 25.5 metres farther in six minutes than the comparison group.
  • The combined rate of death, hospitalisation or stroke was 21.0% with yoga rehab versus 22.8% with standard care — a 1.8 percentage-point difference that was not statistically significant over a median 15 months.
  • For readers: this was a supervised, structured programme delivered by trained practitioners, not a general yoga class — talk to your cardiology team about cardiac rehab options before starting any programme.

A structured yoga-based cardiac rehabilitation programme improved quality of life and walking distance for people living with heart failure, but did not significantly reduce death, hospitalisation or stroke, according to late-breaking findings from the Yoga-CaRe HF trial presented at the American Heart Association Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago. The results were reported by Patient Care Online and in an American Heart Association news release.

What the trial tested

Yoga-CaRe HF was a multicentre, randomised trial conducted across 16 hospitals in India. Between April 2023 and December 2025, investigators recruited 3,547 participants, of whom 3,492 were randomised: 1,737 to yoga-based cardiac rehabilitation and 1,755 to enhanced standard care. Participants had heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, meaning the heart's main pumping chamber pushes out 40% or less of the blood it contains with each beat. The median age was 57 years and 27% were women, Patient Care Online reported.

The intervention combined standardised yoga practices — physical postures, breathing practices and meditation and relaxation tailored to patients' exercise capacity — with health education using a "Healthy Living with Heart Failure" booklet and individualised behaviour goals. Participants attended 20 supervised sessions over three months, followed by one session every three months. The comparison group received three health education sessions over three months and the same booklet.

Quality of life improved; hard outcomes did not reach significance

At three months, the yoga group had an 8.06-point greater improvement on the Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire than the standard-care group (95% CI, -8.87 to -7.24; P<.001), where lower scores indicate better quality of life. Exercise capacity also improved: the yoga group walked 25.5 metres farther in six minutes than the comparison group. Health status on the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire was also better, by 0.05 points, according to Patient Care Online.

The clinical picture was different. Over a median follow-up of 15 months, 364 participants (21.0%) in the yoga group died, were hospitalised or had a stroke, compared with 401 (22.8%) in the standard-care group. In absolute terms that is 1.8 percentage points lower, but the difference was not statistically significant (hazard ratio 0.90; 95% CI, 0.78-1.04; P=.15). A single trial with a non-significant result on this endpoint does not establish that yoga rehab prevents death or hospitalisation.

"Cardiac rehab programs are inaccessible to many, and their uptake is poor in many countries. Innovations are needed to reduce costs, scale up cardiac rehab and make it sustainable."

— Dorairaj Prabhakaran, lead investigator, via the American Heart Association

Limits readers should keep in mind

The American Heart Association release notes that abstracts presented at its scientific meetings are not peer-reviewed and findings are considered preliminary until published in a peer-reviewed journal. The trial could not be blinded — participants knew which programme they were in — and the yoga group had far more supervised contact (20 sessions versus 3), which could have influenced patient-reported outcomes, Patient Care Online noted. The study was conducted entirely in India, where yoga's cultural acceptability may differ from the United States, and the programme was delivered by a board-certified yoga and naturopathy practitioner using a standardised protocol. The results therefore do not generalise to unsupervised yoga or commercial classes.

What this means if you live with heart failure

Cardiac rehabilitation is a guideline-recommended part of heart failure care, but access and uptake are limited. The Yoga-CaRe findings suggest a structured, supervised yoga-based programme may help daily functioning and quality of life alongside usual treatment — not as a replacement for guideline-directed medication or established rehab where it is available. If you or a parent live with heart failure, ask your cardiology team what rehab programmes are covered and available locally before enrolling in any yoga programme, and do not stop prescribed medication on the basis of this trial.
